title.name: Stone by Stone
title.subtitle: Climb and restore the palace of Olite
menu.normal.note: Five hearts for all five climbs.
menu.duo.note: Tied with a rope: help each other up. You only get there together!
menu.solo.note: Alone: use the crates to reach the high ledges.
intro.1: Olite, 1813. The story goes that during the war against Napoleon, the palace of the kings of Navarre burned and fell into ruin.
intro.2: From 1937 it began to be restored. In Master Aitziber's workshop work two apprentices: Íñigo and Maite.
intro.3: Roped together, they'll climb stone by stone and put every part back: battlements, arches, towers...
outro.1: The banner of Navarre flies from the highest tower. The palace of Olite shines again!
outro.2: You can visit it for real today: much of it was rebuilt from 1937 on, following what was left standing.
level.walls.name: The town wall

level.gardens.tip: Old trellises give way, so keep moving! Shoo the storks with your mallet.

level.gallery.tip: Watch out for loose roof tiles! They wobble for a moment before they fall.

level.winds.tip: Gusts of wind push you about. Wait for them to pass before you jump.

level.crowns.where: The very top of the palace
level.crowns.tip: The last climb! Plant the banner of Navarre at the top, together.

fact.title: Did you know?
fact.charles: Charles III the Noble, king of Navarre from 1387 to 1425, enlarged the palace of Olite and made it his grand residence.
fact.gardens: The palace had hanging gardens high on its walls. It is said that orange trees grew there.
fact.gallery: The King's Gallery has Gothic arches carved into the stone like lace, open onto the gardens.
fact.winds: The Tower of the Four Winds is said to take its name from its lookout, open on all four sides.
fact.crowns: The Tower of the Three Crowns is one of the palace's tallest. Its name is thought to come from its stepped top.
fact.fire: The story goes that in 1813 the palace was burned so French troops could not use it.
fact.restore: From 1937 the palace was slowly restored. Part of what you see today was rebuilt in those years.
fact.storks: Every spring, storks nest on the towers and bell towers of southern Navarre.
fact.lions: The story goes that exotic animals, lions among them, were kept at the palace of Olite to amaze the court.
talk.walls.1: We start with the wall. Three carved stones are waiting for their place: battlements, an arrow slit and the shield.
talk.walls.2: Come on, Maite! If I can't reach, I'll climb onto your shoulders.
talk.gardens.1: Up above were the hanging gardens. Give them back their orange tree, their pergola and their cistern.
talk.gardens.2: Orange trees this far north? Now that's unusual!
talk.gallery.1: The King's Gallery had arches carved like lace. Careful: some trapdoors only open while someone stands on a plate.
talk.gallery.2: One stands on the plate, the other goes through. Then swap!
talk.winds.1: The Tower of the Four Winds. Hold on tight: it blows hard up here.
talk.winds.2: We've got the lookout, the weather vane and the spire. Don't drop them!
talk.crowns.1: The last one: the Tower of the Three Crowns. Set its three crowns and plant the banner of Navarre.
talk.crowns.2: Stone by stone, all the way up!
part.crenels.name: Battlements
part.crenels.text: They sheltered the defenders at the top of the wall.
part.slit.name: Arrow slit
part.slit.text: Through this narrow slit you could watch the fields without leaning out.
part.shield.name: Shield of Navarre
part.shield.text: It is said its chains recall the battle of Las Navas de Tolosa, in 1212.
part.orange.name: Orange tree
part.orange.text: It is said orange trees grew in the hanging gardens, a rarity this far north.
part.pergola.name: Pergola
part.pergola.text: Vines and climbers shaded the court's walks.
part.cistern.name: Cistern
part.cistern.text: It stored rainwater for drinking and watering. One of the palace towers is named after it.
part.arch.name: Pointed arch
part.arch.text: Typical of Gothic: it rises higher and weighs less than a round arch.
part.tracery.name: Tracery
part.tracery.text: Stone cut through like lace to decorate windows and arches.
part.plaster.name: Plasterwork
part.plaster.text: Some rooms are thought to have been decorated with plasterwork by Mudéjar craftsmen.
part.lookout.name: Lookout
part.lookout.text: From here the roads were watched and the landscape enjoyed.
part.vane.name: Weather vane
part.vane.text: It turns with the wind and shows where it blows from.
part.spire.name: Spire roof
part.spire.text: Some towers were topped with pointed roofs called spires.
part.crown1.name: First crown
part.crown1.text: Each crown is a ring of battlements narrower than the one below.
part.crown2.name: Second crown
part.crown2.text: From up here you can see much of southern Navarre.
part.crown3.name: Third crown
part.crown3.text: The tower is thought to take its name from these three stepped crowns.
reveal.title: Then and now
level.walls.then: The wall protected the palace and the town.
level.walls.ruin: Fallen battlements and stones blackened by fire.
level.walls.now: The restored wall surrounds the palace again.
level.gardens.then: Green terraces with orange trees, high on the palace.
level.gardens.ruin: The terraces were left dry and full of rubble.
level.gardens.now: The palace has tree-filled courtyards again, like the Mulberry Courtyard.
level.gallery.then: The court strolled beneath its lacework arches.
level.gallery.now: The Gothic arches are back in place.
level.winds.then: A lookout open to the four winds.
level.winds.ruin: The tower was left hollow and roofless.
level.winds.now: The tower looks out over the land again.
level.crowns.then: The royal banner flew from the very top.
level.crowns.now: Today it is one of the palace's most visited towers.
msg.carry: Take it to its gap, the one glowing on the wall!
msg.plate: One holds the plate, the other goes through
